panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial CT of an 8-year-old girl showing a destructive lesion of the medial right clavicle with periosteal reaction and soft tissue swelling; caption explicitly states findings are consistent with CRMO. B: 3D CT reformat of the same patient showing the clavicular lesion (arrow); caption attributes findings to CRMO. C: Axial T2 STIR MRI showing marrow signal abnormality of the medial right clavicle with periosteal fluid and soft tissue edema, consistent with CRMO osteitis. D: Whole-body MRI-STIR demonstrating multifocal metaphyseal lesions in addition to the clavicular lesion, supporting the CRMO diagnosis stated in the caption.

panels.figure_caption: An 8-year-old girl presented with a painful lump on the right clavicle. Axial (A) and 3D reformats (B) computed tomography images demonstrate a destructive lesion in the medial aspect of the right clavicle associated with periosteal reaction and soft tissue swelling (arrow in a/b). Axial T2 STIR magnetic resonance image (C) showed a marked signal abnormality involving the medial aspect of the right clavicle with associated periosteal fluid and soft tissue edema. Total body MRI-STIR sequences (D) showed additional lesions in the proximal right (arrow) and left (arrowhead) humeral metaphysis, right iliac crest (not shown)and left greater trochanter (not shown). Findings are consistent with CRMO following a Whole Body MRI.

in_text_mentions: hs were obtained from 6 patients with CRMO, with no evidence of lesions in 3 of them. In the remaining 3 patients, radiography revealed signs of bone destruction, such as osteosclerosis or osteolytic lesions (Fig. 1). CT scans were performed in 3 patients, revealing lytic lesions and sclerosis with hypodense shadowing in the medullary cavity (Fig. 2). MRI was conducted on all 7 patients who exhibited multiple foci of bone marrow edema, accompanied by high signal changes on T2-weighted images (Figs. 3 and 4), predominantly located in the epiphysis of the long bones, with a few in the diaphysis.

in_text_mentions: uch as low-grade fever and malaise and elevated acute phase proteins) cannot be found, even during attacks. In these cases, the diagnosis of CNO can be made, combining clinical findings (localized bone pain, swelling, and warmth in the affected areas) and laboratory tests (including testing for mycobacteria) with radiographic techniques. The presence of osteolytic lesions with surrounding sclerosis in X-ray imaging, supplemented by computerized tomography (CT) and/or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), is usually helpful (Figure 1). Silent asymptomatic lesions frequently appear on nuclear scans.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Real patient axial T2 STIR MRI of the mandible in a 9-year-old girl showing marrow edema of the right mandibular ramus, a classic CRMO lesion; caption and article title attribute findings to CRMO. B: Real patient axial CT showing smooth periosteal reaction of the right hemimandible in the same 9-year-old CRMO case; periostitis/periosteal reaction is a recognized CRMO feature per in-text mentions, though not in the allowed vocabulary so it is listed as a proposed finding. C: Real patient coronal CT showing smooth periosteal reaction of the right hemimandible in the same 9-year-old CRMO case; periosteal reaction is a recognized CRMO feature per in-text mentions, listed as a proposed finding since it is absent from the vocabulary. D: Real patient axial STIR MRI of the pelvis showing hyperintense marrow signal in the right femoral neck, an additional silent focus on whole-body MRI consistent with multifocal CRMO in a 9-year-old child....

panels.figure_caption: A 9-year-old girl presented with 10 days of right cheek swelling. (B) axial computed tomography and (C) coronal computed tomography images demonstrate smooth periosteal reaction in the right hemi mandible. No associated soft tissue mass or periodontal abscess. Axial (D) and sagittal (E) MRI STIR images demonstrate another focus of hyperintensity in the posterior aspect of the right femoral neck (arrow in D), the distal tibial metaphyses (arrow in e), and the right first (arrowhead in e) and second metatarsals (not shown). Findings are consistent with CRMO following a Whole Body MRI.

in_text_mentions: hs were obtained from 6 patients with CRMO, with no evidence of lesions in 3 of them. In the remaining 3 patients, radiography revealed signs of bone destruction, such as osteosclerosis or osteolytic lesions (Fig. 1). CT scans were performed in 3 patients, revealing lytic lesions and sclerosis with hypodense shadowing in the medullary cavity (Fig. 2). MRI was conducted on all 7 patients who exhibited multiple foci of bone marrow edema, accompanied by high signal changes on T2-weighted images (Figs. 3 and 4), predominantly located in the epiphysis of the long bones, with a few in the diaphysis.

in_text_mentions: Schematically, as explained previously, CRMO mainly consists of osseous lesions, whereas JSpA first includes joint anomalies, leading secondarily to osseous changes. In both diseases, MRI allows the visualization of most of the osteoarticular changes, including (1) bone marrow lesions, especially when using coronal T1-weighted and STIR sequences in addition to axial STIR images (Figure 4 and Figure 5), and (2) inflammatory lesions of the axial joints, which are best visualized on T1 sequences and include erosion, sclerosis, fat metaplasia, backfill and ankyloses [31].
CRMO, SAPHO and JSpA can show similarities in radiological findings (Figure 4 and Figure 5).

plate_findings.evidence: STIR-weighted images show diaphyseal edematous bone marrow involvement, periostal reaction of the left humerus

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Coronal STIR MRI of a 12-year-old girl with known CRMO showing diaphyseal bone marrow edema and periosteal reaction of the left humerus (yellow arrow). Real human-patient radiology image of a CRMO lesion; diaphyseal involvement is noted in-text as an uncommon presentation (one case), hence variant. b: Axial MRI of the same 12-year-old CRMO patient showing large homogeneous bony involvement of the left humerus lesion. Real human-patient image of CRMO; diaphyseal location is a less common (variant) presentation per in-text. c: Axial DWI (b=800) MRI of the same CRMO patient showing signal alteration at the humeral lesion site. Real human-patient radiology image supporting CRMO bone involvement; variant diaphyseal presentation. d: Axial ADC map of the same CRMO patient showing increased ADC at the corresponding humeral lesion site. Real human-patient radiology image of CRMO; variant diaphyseal presentation.

panels.figure_caption: MR images of 12-year old girl with known CRMO. a) STIR-weighted images show diaphyseal edematous bone marrow involvement, periostal reaction of the left humerus b) axial series showing large and homogenous bony involvement c) signal alteration in DWI b = 800 images d) ADC increase at the corresponding site.
in_text_mentions: Most lesions appeared as asymmetric, ill- and irregular- defined changes in the bone marrow with a hyperintense appearance in STIR images. Foci were typically settled in metaphyseal and epiphyseal regions adjacent to a growth plate of tubular bones, as well as in the sacrum, the spine and the pelvis. There was one case of diaphyseal involvement, representing as a huge lesion with periostal reaction of the left humerus (Fig 1).

Skeletal edema detected in STIR images showed up as focal or diffuse area of high-signal intensity on high b-value and also a high ADC-value in WB-DWI (Figs 1–3) in most of our cases. In comparing the apparent diffusion coefficient value of the signal alteration site and the values of the corresponding opposite/ healthy side, one can detect that the apparent diffusion coefficient value of the lesions are relatively higher compared to the healthy side (Table 3). panels.rationale: Whole-body bone scintigraphy (panel A, stored as the complete single image) from a case of nonbacterial osteitis of the clavicle, i.e. the CRMO spectrum, showing a single intense radiotracer 'hot spot' in the right clavicle, a classic CRMO site. Real patient image; no third-party restriction indicated. Disease attribution rests on the disease-focused article title ('Nonbacterial osteitis of the clavicle') plus the specific captioned manifestation (clavicular hot spot), not on the broad topic alone. The hot spot represents a musculoskeletal inflammatory lesion (osteitis) on whole-body skeletal imaging, so it is mapped to the whole-body musculoskeletal-inflammation finding key; the exact scintigraphic manifestation is recorded in proposed_findings because no dedicated scintigraphy key exists. The presentation was monofocal ('a multifocal disease was unlikely'), a recognized less-common form of the CRMO/NBO spectrum, hence typicality 'variant'; the vocabulary defines no subtype, so subtype is null. Bone scintigraphy has no dedicated modality enum value, so modality is 'other'. No age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or in-text, so both are unknown/null; no skin is shown, so skin_tone is null. Confidence reflects solid disease attribution tempered by the modality/multiplicity mismatch of the mapped finding.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Coronal whole-body STIR MRI explicitly captioned as CRMO, showing multifocal bone marrow edema in right lower femur, right upper tibia, and left lower tibia metaphysis with joint effusion—classic CRMO long-bone involvement. b: Sagittal STIR MRI of the same captioned CRMO patient showing periosseous edema in the interspinous space; axial/spine involvement is a recognized but less common (variant) site in CRMO, supporting multifocal attribution.
panels.attribution_text: Koné-Paut et al. Chronic Recurrent Multifocal Osteomyelitis (CRMO) and Juvenile Spondyloarthritis (JSpA): To What Extent Are They Related?. Journal of clinical medicine 2023. doi:10.3390/jcm12020453. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Whole body MRI, same patient 18 months later, CRMO with probable overlapping SpA. Asymmetrical position during MRI acquisition due to intense pain. Coronal plane in (a) STIR-weighted sequence showing bone marrow edema in the right lower femur and right upper tibia (arrow), associated with joint effusion (arrowhead) and bone marrow edema in the metaphysis of the left lower tibia (small arrowhead). Sagittal plane in (b) STIR-weighted sequence showing periosseous edema in the interspinous space (arrows).
in_text_mentions: Schematically, as explained previously, CRMO mainly consists of osseous lesions, whereas JSpA first includes joint anomalies, leading secondarily to osseous changes. In both diseases, MRI allows the visualization of most of the osteoarticular changes, including (1) bone marrow lesions, especially when using coronal T1-weighted and STIR sequences in addition to axial STIR images (Figure 4 and Figure 5), and (2) inflammatory lesions of the axial joints, which are best visualized on T1 sequences and include erosion, sclerosis, fat metaplasia, backfill and ankyloses [31].
CRMO, SAPHO and JSpA can show similarities in radiological findings (Figure 4 and Figure 5).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Axial chest CT from a CRMO case report demonstrating sclerosis of the sternum and manubrium with sternoclavicular erosions; the in-text CT description confirms medial clavicular expansion/sclerosis with small lytic areas, a classic anterior chest-wall CRMO pattern. B: PET-CT fusion image from the same CRMO patient showing diffuse abnormal hypermetabolic uptake throughout the manubrium sternum with expansion of the manubrium and intense activity at the manubrial-sternal junction, corresponding to the sclerotic anterior chest-wall lesions seen on CT. in_text_mentions: asound examination showed no synovitis, though a small amount of joint fluid was present; puncture fluid culture was also negative. Although MRI showed significant bone marrow edema, the absence of active synovitis on ultrasound made juvenile idiopathic arthritis unlikely. MRI (Short Tau Inversion Recovery) demonstrated bone marrow edema, suggesting osteomyelitis (Figure 1). Due to immunosuppression, hematogenous bacterial osteomyelitis was suspected, and empirical antibiotics were initiated. As C-reactive protein levels gradually decreased and symptoms resolved, antibiotics were discontinued.

radiographic appearance. As in our presented case, the lesions can also involve the diaphysis, which may result from spread of an earlier metaphyseal lesion [5]. Diaphyseal lesions are characterized by lytic destructive areas and periosteal reaction, which heal with sclerosis and hyperostosis [5, 9]. Recurrent active lesions will progressively lay down further bone adding to the expansion and sclerotic appearance [10] (Figure 1). Active diaphyseal lesions may show small lytic areas with regions of new bone formation [5], a finding that is better seen on the CT (Figure 2) of our presented case.

escribed under radiographic assessment, with the advantage of detecting subtle bone destruction, especially in anatomically difficult sites like the sternum, spine, and pelvis. Sclerosis and periosteal reaction may also be seen [5]. As shown in the presented case, small lytic areas of active disease can be identified on the CT (Figure 2). Its major drawback is the significant radiation exposure, which must be considered especially in children [6]. A CT of the chest was also obtained in our patient to rule out metastatic disease as Ewing's sarcoma was part of the working differential diagnosis.

panels.figure_caption: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) in a 20-year-old male presented with recurrent left foot pain and swelling. Findings/technique- Non-contrast MRI (3T) of left foot with PDFS sequences in (a) sagittal, (b) coronal and (c) axial sections showing hyperintense marrow signal involving first metatarsal bone with significant cortical thickening and associated adjacent soft tissue edema.
in_text_mentions: the left foot showed altered abnormal signals within the shaft of the first metatarsal with the widening of the bone and cortical thickening without break in bony cortices. The moderate hyperintense signal was seen surrounding the bone which was extending in the adjacent soft tissues and lumbricals. The first metatarso-phalangeal joint was distended with fluid and both the collateral ligaments were displaced. A few subchondral cysts were noted in the calcaneum, fourth, and fifth proximal metatarsals with surrounding marrow edema. Surrounding diffuse subcutaneous edema was also seen (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: HE-stained human bone biopsy from a CRMO patient in the early phase showing predominant neutrophilic infiltrate (arrows), matching the vocabulary finding of neutrophilic osteitis; caption and in-text explicitly attribute the panel to CRMO. B: HE-stained human bone biopsy showing the chronic inflammatory stage of CRMO with monocyte, lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltration; caption and in-text explicitly attribute it to CRMO. The chronic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate is not covered by the vocabulary, so it is recorded as a proposed finding. C: HE-stained human bone biopsy of the late chronic fibrosing stage of CRMO; caption and in-text explicitly attribute the panel to CRMO and describe fibrosis in late phases. Fibrosis is not in the allowed vocabulary, so it is recorded as a proposed finding.

panels.figure_caption: Histological appearance of early and late stages of CRMO. A) Hematoxylin and eosin (HE) stained bone biopsy in the early phase of CRMO. Neutrophils and monocytes (arrows) are the predominant cell types. B) HE stained bone biopsy showing chronic inflammation in CRMO with monocytes, lymphocytes and plasma cell infiltration. C) HE stained biopsy of the late chronic fibrosing stage in CRMO.

in_text_mentions: hs were obtained from 6 patients with CRMO, with no evidence of lesions in 3 of them. In the remaining 3 patients, radiography revealed signs of bone destruction, such as osteosclerosis or osteolytic lesions (Fig. 1). CT scans were performed in 3 patients, revealing lytic lesions and sclerosis with hypodense shadowing in the medullary cavity (Fig. 2). MRI was conducted on all 7 patients who exhibited multiple foci of bone marrow edema, accompanied by high signal changes on T2-weighted images (Figs. 3 and 4), predominantly located in the epiphysis of the long bones, with a few in the diaphysis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Low-power H&E of bone biopsy explicitly captioned as CRMO histopathology showing nonbacterial osteomyelitis; human patient tissue with sterile inflammatory infiltrate consistent with neutrophilic osteitis. B: High-power H&E of the same CRMO bone biopsy showing the mixed inflammatory infiltrate of nonbacterial osteomyelitis; classic histopathology of the target disease. C: CD117 immunostaining of the CRMO bone biopsy showing mast cell positivity; caption and in-text explicitly link this stain to the CRMO pathology workup. Mast cell infiltrate is a recognized but less prominent finding, hence variant. D: Tryptase immunostaining of the CRMO bone biopsy confirming mast cell infiltrate; caption and in-text explicitly support this as part of the CRMO bone pathology workup. Recognized but less common finding, hence variant.

panels.rationale: Whole-body 18-FDG PET scan of the child patient from the CRMO case report, showing faint multifocal tracer uptake in the right humeral head and right femoral head (black arrows), representing multifocal osteitis/musculoskeletal inflammation that confirmed the prior MRI findings and excluded malignancy. Disease attribution to chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis is directly supported by the article title and in-text mentions; no other disease is identified for this panel, no third-party copyright is indicated, and the image is a real patient scan. The finding maps to the vocabulary entry for multifocal musculoskeletal inflammation/multifocal osteitis (confirmed by PET rather than MRI). Black arrows are present as annotations.

In order to exclude an infectious osteomyelitis or a malignant tumor, the patient also underwent to a PET-CT showing the presence of a pathological high-uptake of the lesion. Patient’s right shoulder biopsy showed bone infiltration by lymphocytes and neutrophils. No neoplastic cells were identified. All cultures were negative. plate_findings.evidence: FDG/PET imaging was performed for a systemic search; increased uptake in the right proximal tibia (SUVmax 4.90), right proximal clavicle (SUVmax 3.20), and distal humerus (SUVmax 3.20)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Whole-body FDG PET shows multifocal increased bone uptake in a patient with CRMO. B: Axial PET/CT shows focal FDG avidity in the right proximal tibia, a CRMO lesion. C: Axial PET/CT shows focal FDG avidity in the right proximal clavicle, consistent with CRMO involvement. D: Axial PET/CT shows focal FDG avidity in the distal humerus, consistent with CRMO involvement.
panels.attribution_text: Hirota et al. Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography Evaluation of Chronic Recurrent Multifocal Osteomyelitis.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.69735. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: FDG/PET imaging was performed for a systemic search (A), which revealed increased uptake in the right proximal tibia (SUVmax 4.90) (B), right proximal clavicle (SUVmax 3.20) (C), and distal humerus (SUVmax 3.20) (D) (red and yellow arrow).
in_text_mentions: Four months post-discharge, she developed swelling and sharp pain in her clavicle and elbow. MRI of the clavicle showed findings consistent with those of the tibia. Given the potential for undetected malignant areas in the tibial lesion, an FDG/PET was performed for a systemic evaluation. The imaging revealed increased 18FDG uptake in the right proximal tibia (maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) 4.90), right proximal clavicle (SUVmax 3.20), and distal humerus (SUVmax 3.20) (Figure 5).

plate_findings.evidence: suspected septic arthritis and osteomyelitis involving the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5)
Full-body magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multifocal infectious/inflammatory changes ... involving the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) and the left iliac bone (Figures 2A, 2B)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial MRI slice from a full-body MRI in a child with CRMO (article title: 'Scurvy in the Modern Era: Revisiting a Forgotten Diagnosis in a Child With Chronic Recurrent Multifocal Osteomyelitis') showing inflammatory changes/osteomyelitis of the left L5 posterior elements, consistent with the multifocal musculoskeletal inflammation of CRMO. Arrows annotate the lesion. B: Axial MRI slice from a full-body MRI in a child with CRMO showing osteomyelitis of the iliac bones, part of the multifocal inflammatory bone disease. Arrows annotate the iliac lesions.
panels.attribution_text: Abou Zeid et al. Scurvy in the Modern Era: Revisiting a Forgotten Diagnosis in a Child With Chronic Recurrent Multifocal Osteomyelitis.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.91964. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Full-body MRI showing septic arthritis of the left aspect of the L5 posterior elements (A) and iliac bones (B) with osteomyelitis (yellow arrows).
in_text_mentions: h an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 19 mm/hour (reference range: 0-15 mm/hour) and C-reactive protein of 4 mg/dL (reference range: 0.0- 2.5 mg/L). Full-body magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multifocal infectious/inflammatory changes in the femoral heads bilaterally and in multiple anterior and posterior ribs, with additional findings of pseudoarthrosis and suspected septic arthritis and osteomyelitis involving the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) and the left iliac bone (Figures 2A, 2B). Differential diagnoses included multifocal osteomyelitis with septic arthritis, CRMO, and malignancy.

panels.body_site: right clavicle and lower neck/upper chest
panels.rationale: Clinical photograph showing visible swelling of the right clavicle in a patient with chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, consistent with the article title and caption. The clavicle is a classic site of involvement in CRMO.
panels.attribution_text: Bleckwenn et al. Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis manifested as painful clavicular swelling: a case report.. BMC research notes 2014. doi:10.1186/1756-0500-7-786. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Swelling of the right clavicle – the abnormality has not changed in appearance since the first contact with the patient.
in_text_mentions: The examination revealed a distinct swelling of the clavicle (Figure 1). On palpation it proved to be a hard, non-displaceable lesion measuring 8 × 5 cm. In comparison with the left clavicle a notably higher temperature could be detected in the swollen region. A systematic examination yielded no other visible findings. In the presence of clavicular swelling, it is especially important to rule out a malignancy (Table 1).Figure 1 Swelling of the right clavicle – the abnormality has not changed in appearance since the first contact with the patient.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real human-patient H&E sternum biopsy from a case report whose title and in-text establish chronic recurrent multififocal osteomyelitis; the sternum is a classic CRMO site and the captioned thickened trabeculae, medullary fibrosis and sterile mononuclear inflammatory collections are typical chronic CRMO histology. Inflammatory infiltrate in bone biopsy is captured by the vocabulary histology finding; specific features not in the vocabulary are listed as proposed findings. B: Real human-patient H&E biopsy of the sternoclavicular joint from the same CRMO case; the sternoclavicular joint is a characteristic CRMO location and the captioned dense fibrous tissue with focal sterile lymphoplasmacytic collections is typical chronic CRMO histology. Inflammatory infiltrate in the biopsy is captured by the vocabulary histology finding; additional specific features are listed as proposed findings.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial T1-weighted MRI of the proximal tibia metaphysis from an article focused on chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis; shows a hypointense bone lesion consistent with CRMO-related marrow abnormality. B: Axial T2-weighted MRI demonstrates a hyperintense metaphyseal lesion, a typical CRMO MRI manifestation (marrow edema/increased signal). C: Axial gadolinium-enhanced MRI shows enhancement within the proximal tibial metaphyseal lesion, consistent with active CRMO inflammation. D: Sagittal post-contrast MRI confirms enhancing metaphyseal lesion in the setting of CRMO, with arrow indicating the abnormality.

plate_findings.evidence: caption: 'Radiographs showing chronic osteomyelitis'; visual: distal radial/ulnar metaphyseal lucency with surrounding sclerosis

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real-patient wrist radiograph from the CRMO case report; the caption and in-text state that wrist radiographs revealed chronic osteomyelitis in the course of recurrent multifocal disease, and the image shows metaphyseal (distal radius/ulna) lytic/sclerotic change consistent with CRMO rather than PSC (no biliary finding is imaged). Skeletally immature bones and the article title ('...in a Child') support a child patient; no skin or ethnicity is assessable on a radiograph. Included because it is a genuine patient image showing a specific CRMO manifestation. B: Contralateral wrist radiograph in the same CRMO patient. Although clinically asymptomatic, the caption explicitly states the radiographs showed chronic osteomyelitis, i.e. a silent CRMO bone lesion; this is not a normal/control image because radiographic osteomyelitis is present. Same metaphyseal distal radius/ulna lytic/sclerotic CRMO manifestation. Child per article title and open...

JMA journal 2025. doi:10.31662/jmaj.2025-0196. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Radiograph of both wrists performed 6 months after the initial visit. Radiographs showing chronic osteomyelitis, though the contralateral wrist was asymptomatic.
in_text_mentions: Six months later, wrist pain recurred. Radiographs of both wrists revealed chronic osteomyelitis, although the contralateral wrist remained asymptomatic (Figure 2). Given the patient’s immunosuppression state, a bacterial flare-up was suspected, and antibiotics were resumed. Symptoms again resolved. One year and 6 months later, the patient developed right heel pain, and MRI confirmed bone marrow edema (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Genuine patient dynamic MRI of the sacrum; the captioned S1-S2 and right S1 foramen edema matches CRMO-associated bone marrow edema, and the CRMO-focused article title supports attribution despite the unconfirmed osteoid osteoma impression.

panels.figure_caption: Dynamic MRI showing edema centered on the S1‐S2 disc, lateralized to the right of the midline, extending into the right S1 foramen.
in_text_mentions: A subsequent dynamic MRI revealed edema centered on the S1‐S2 disc, lateralized to the right side of the midline, and extending into the right S1 foramen (Figure 1). The radiologist’s interpretation favored an osteoid osteoma, though the diagnosis was not confirmed. The patient was started on a regimen of etoricoxib 60 mg per day and observed for 2 months, during which he experienced significant pain relief.

plate_findings.evidence: infiltrating inflammatory cells

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: H&E bone biopsy panel from a patient with CRMO; caption documents inflammatory cell infiltration and collagen fiber proliferation, consistent with neutrophilic osteitis in CRMO. B: H&E bone biopsy panel from a patient with CRMO; caption documents inflammatory cell infiltration and collagen fiber proliferation, consistent with neutrophilic osteitis in CRMO.
panels.attribution_text: Hirota et al. Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography Evaluation of Chronic Recurrent Multifocal Osteomyelitis.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.69735. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: A histological analysis of the primary tumor reveals infiltrating inflammatory cells, proliferating collagen fibers, and no atypical cells (A and B).
in_text_mentions: All other biochemical and serologic tests were normal. Based on these hematological investigations and imaging findings, osteomyelitis was initially suspected. The patient was treated with antibiotics (cefcapene pivoxil [CFPN-PI]) for 20 days, but there was no improvement. Consequently, the possibility of malignant bone tumors, such as Ewing's sarcoma, was considered. An incisional biopsy was performed, and the histological analysis revealed infiltration of inflammatory cells, proliferation of collagen fibers, and the absence of atypical cells (Figure 4).

plate_findings.evidence: widening of bone with subtle thickening of cortex and sclerosis involving the distal epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis of the first metatarsal bone of the left foot

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Dorso-plantar radiograph of both feet in a 20-year-old male with CRMO shows bone widening, cortical thickening and sclerosis of the left first metatarsal involving epiphysis, metaphysis and diaphysis; white arrow marks the lesion. Real patient diagnostic radiograph directly attributed to CRMO by caption and disease-focused article title. b: Postero-anterior radiograph of both hands in a 20-year-old male with CRMO shows bone widening, cortical thickening and sclerosis of the right third metacarpal; white arrow marks the lesion. Real patient diagnostic radiograph directly attributed to CRMO by caption and disease-focused article title.
panels.attribution_text: Waghmode et al. A Case of Sterile Osteomyelitis: Chronic Recurrent Multifocal Osteomyelitis (CRMO).. Cureus 2022. doi:10.7759/cureus.26370. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) in a 20-year-old male presented with recurrent right hand and left foot pain. Findings/technique- (a) Dorso-plantar radiograph of both feet showing widening of bone with subtle thickening of cortex and sclerosis involving the distal epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis of the first metatarsal bone of the left foot. (b) Postero-anterior radiographs of both hands show similar features involving the shaft and distal end of the right third metacarpal with comparatively more evident sclerosis. The findings are more evident when compared to the contralateral normal side.
in_text_mentions: Due to the recent aggravation of symptoms, he came to a tertiary care center for detailed investigation. On admission, radiographs of all the limbs were done and there were significant findings detected in the right hand and left foot. The head and shaft of the third metacarpal appeared widened with cortical thickening and surrounding soft tissue edema (Figure 1a). Similar findings were detected on the first metatarsal of the right foot showing diaphyseal widening with areas of sclerosis and cortical thickening (Figure 1b).

panels.rationale: Single-panel radiograph of both legs from an article titled 'Unusual case of chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis.' A white arrow marks hyperostosis of the left tibial metaphysis, and the in-text describes hyperostosis and sclerosis of the tibial metaphysis with periosteal reaction, consistent with CRMO. It is a real human-patient image with no third-party copyright. The only metaphyseal radiographic vocabulary key specifies osteolytic lesions, whereas the image shows hyperostosis/sclerosis, so the precise features are also recorded as proposed_findings; the metaphyseal key is used for the metaphyseal bone-lesion localization. No age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or provided in-text.

panels.rationale: Sagittal MRI of the spine showing abnormal enhancement/signal of the vertebral bodies, i.e. marrow edema/osteitis on MRI, a recognized manifestation of chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis. The caption is neutral (does not name another disease), the article's configured/primary topic disease is CRMO, and the prior caption triage kept this as a single-disease radiology image. Confidence is moderated because the article ultimately diagnoses primary T-cell rich B-cell lymphoma of bone that was masquerading as CRMO, so the vertebral enhancement in this specific patient was due to lymphoma mimicking CRMO rather than biopsy-proven CRMO.

in_text_mentions: left clavicle with irregularities in the bone cortex. MRI showed an extensive lesion measuring 9 x 2 x 2 cm located at the medial end of the left clavicle and extending to the acromioclavicular joint (Figure 3). A needle biopsy was initially performed, suspected bone infection and the child received antibiotics with no recovery and appearance of important periosteal apposition on radiographs (Figure 4). Ewing's sarcoma was still suspected and a second open biopsy was performed two weeks later as well as the culture of mycobacteria and the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for the Koch bacillus.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial MRI of the skull and orbits from a CRMO case report ('Unusual onset of a case of chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis') showing a subacute inflammatory process of the left orbital region with periorbital soft-tissue and bone involvement, directly attributed to CRMO by the caption and in-text context. Orbital/skull onset is an unusual CRMO presentation, hence atypical. Red arrow annotates the affected left orbital region. B: Companion axial MRI slice/sequence of the same CRMO case, with green circle highlighting the left orbital inflammatory lesion and red arrow pointing to the periorbital soft-tissue involvement. Caption and in-text context attribute the subacute bone and soft-tissue inflammation to CRMO; orbital onset is unusual, hence atypical.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Anteroposterior radiograph of the left femur from a CRMO case report; caption and in-text describe moth-eaten metaphyseal osteolysis with Codman triangle periosteal reaction and soft-tissue edema, an aggressive radiological appearance that mimicked a malignant bone tumor, which is atypical for CRMO. Real human-patient image of the target disease with a specific captioned manifestation. B: Lateral radiograph of the left femur from the same CRMO case; caption groups it with panel A describing moth-eaten metaphyseal osteolysis with Codman triangle periosteal reaction and soft-tissue edema mimicking a malignant bone tumor, an atypical CRMO presentation. Real human-patient image of the target disease with a specific captioned manifestation.

panels.rationale: Axial MRI of the head from a case report titled 'Unusual case of chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis.' The caption and in-text explicitly state a new CRMO lesion in the right periorbital region with hyperostosis of the frontal bone measured at 27.3 mm. This is a real patient image showing a specific CRMO manifestation (frontal bone hyperostosis), making it includable. The article labels the case as unusual, and the periorbital/frontal bone location is an uncommon site for CRMO, so typicality is atypical. The hyperostosis itself is not in the allowed vocabulary and is placed in proposed_findings; bone marrow edema is supported as the MRI correlate of the captioned CRMO lesion.

Pathology revealed dense bone with reactive changes and mild marrow fibrosis; changes noted to be consistent with a chronic inflammatory process such as chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) (Figures 6 and 7); and no evidence of Paget's disease or neoplasm. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: AP radiograph from a case report titled geriatric CRMO mimicking multifocal multiple myeloma; panel shows captioned femoral diaphyseal infiltrative lesion with cortical destruction and periosteal reaction. Attribution to CRMO is supported by the disease-focused article title and specific captioned bone manifestation, though the in-text notes the imaging gestalt suggested multiple myeloma. B: Lateral radiograph from a CRMO case report; shows the captioned right proximal femoral diaphyseal lesion with cortical destruction and periosteal reaction. Disease attribution relies on the CRMO-focused article title plus specific captioned bone manifestation. C: Coronal CT panel from a CRMO case report; demonstrates the captioned diaphyseal cortical destruction and periosteal reaction with osseous proliferation. Article title supports CRMO attribution; green arrow annotation present. D: Axial CT panel from a CRMO case report; shows the captioned...
